chunks: My father (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated to us. He said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us. He said: Ibrahim ibn Hashim narrated to us from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Najran from Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him). He said:

Ali (peace be upon him) would go out every morning and patrol the marketplaces of Kufa, one market at a time. With him was a whip on his shoulder, and it had two strips, and it was called al-Sabiba. He would stand at every market and call out: O merchants! Seek goodness [from Allah], conclude each transaction with ease, be close to the consumers, adorn yourselves with forbearance, abstain from lying and false oaths, desist from injustice, relieve the oppressed, do not come close to usury, maintain proper measurement and balance, do not undervalue the people's things, and do not spread corruption in the land. He would roam through all the markets of Kufa and say this. Then he would say: Pleasure will fade away from those who attained its sweetness from the forbidden, and what remains is sin and disgrace. Harsh consequences remain in its aftermath — there is no good in a pleasure after which comes the Fire.

key_terms.استخارة: Seeking goodness/guidance from Allah before transactions
key_terms.السبيبة: Al-Sabiba; the name of Ali's whip with two strips
key_terms.الكيل والميزان: Measurement and balance; fair trade practices
key_terms.ربا: Usury; charging interest on loans, strictly forbidden in Islam

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali patrol the markets of Kufa and what ethical guidelines did he give to merchants?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) narrates that Imam Ali (AS) would patrol the markets of Kufa every morning carrying a whip called al-Sabiba. He would stand at each market and admonish the merchants with comprehensive ethical guidelines: seeking goodness from Allah, treating customers with ease and forbearance, abstaining from lying, false oaths, injustice, usury, and cheating in measurements. He would conclude with poetry warning that forbidden pleasures fade but sin and the Fire remain.
